label: Psychology
title: Nobody Is Watching You as Closely as You Think – The Spotlight Effect
thumbnail_text: Nobody is watching you that closely
description: Why do we feel so watched, judged and exposed – when most people barely notice us? In this calm video essay we look at the famous Barry Manilow T-shirt study behind the spotlight effect, the illusion of transparency, the surprising 'liking gap' after conversations, and what Marcus Aurelius and Epictetus said about living by other people's opinions. Plus a simple way to step out of the imaginary spotlight.

sections.text:
You walk into a room and trip over a step. Or you say something slightly awkward in a meeting. For the rest of the day, the moment keeps replaying in your head. Everyone must have noticed. Everyone must be thinking about it.

But here is the strange thing. Ask the others a few hours later, and most of them will not remember it at all.

Psychologists have a name for this gap between how visible we feel and how visible we really are. And once you understand it, a lot of quiet pressure begins to lift.

sections.heading: The T-Shirt Experiment
sections.text:
In the late 1990s, the psychologist Thomas Gilovich and his colleagues at Cornell University ran an experiment that has since become a classic.

They asked students to put on a T-shirt with a large picture of the singer Barry Manilow. For students at the time, this was not exactly a cool choice. Then each student walked into a room where other participants were already sitting, stayed briefly, and left again.

Afterwards, the students were asked to estimate how many people in the room had noticed who was on their shirt. They guessed about half. In reality, only around a quarter could say.

The researchers called this the spotlight effect. We tend to believe that a social spotlight follows us around, lighting up our appearance, our mistakes, and our awkward moments. But most of the time, that spotlight is far dimmer than we imagine.

sections.heading: Why We Feel So Visible
sections.text:
Why does this happen? Part of the answer is simple. You are the center of your own experience. You have spent your whole life looking out from behind your own eyes. You know every detail of your shirt, your voice, your little mistake, because you live inside them.

Other people are in exactly the same position. They are busy being the center of their own experience. They are thinking about their own shirt, their own meeting, their own awkward moment.

When we judge how others see us, we start from our own vivid inner picture, and we do not adjust enough. Gilovich described this as a kind of anchoring. Our own perspective is the starting point, and we fail to move far enough away from it.

There is a close cousin of this effect, which Gilovich and his colleagues called the illusion of transparency. We tend to believe that our inner states are written on our faces. That others can see our nervousness, our embarrassment, our doubt. In their studies, people who were nervous while speaking, or who were telling a small lie, consistently overestimated how much others could see.

sections.heading: The Liking Gap
sections.text:
There is one more finding that belongs here, and it is perhaps the most comforting.

In 2018, the psychologist Erica Boothby and her colleagues studied what happens after people have a conversation with someone they have just met. Afterwards, both people rated how much they liked the other person, and how much they thought the other person liked them.

Again and again, people underestimated how much their conversation partner had enjoyed talking with them. The researchers called this the liking gap. While we replay our clumsy sentences and awkward pauses, the other person is often walking away with a warmer impression than we think.

In other words, the spotlight effect does not only make us overestimate how much others notice our mistakes. It also hides from us how kindly we are often seen.

sections.heading: What the Stoics Noticed

quote.lead: Long before these experiments, Marcus Aurelius noticed a strange contradiction in human nature.
quote.text: I have often wondered how it is that every man loves himself more than all the rest of men, but yet sets less value on his own opinion of himself than on the opinion of others.
quote.author: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations XII.4

sections.text:
The Stoics did not have the word spotlight effect. But they knew how much of our peace we hand over to the imagined judgments of others.

Epictetus was even more direct. In his Handbook, he advises that if you want to make progress, you must be willing to be thought foolish about external things. Not because other people do not matter, but because their opinions are not in your control. If your calm depends on how you look in every moment, you will never be calm.

There is a freedom in this. When you realise that most people are not watching you very closely, and that you cannot control what they think anyway, you can turn your attention back to what is actually yours. Your intention. Your effort. The way you treat the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Stepping Out of the Spotlight
sections.text:
So what can you do the next time you feel exposed? Here are three small steps.

First, name it. Simply knowing about the spotlight effect can help. In one study, Kenneth Savitsky and Thomas Gilovich told nervous speakers about the illusion of transparency before they gave a short talk. Those speakers felt less anxious, and their talks were rated as better by observers.

Second, switch perspectives. Ask yourself: if a friend had done exactly the same thing, would I still be thinking about it tonight? Almost always, the answer is no. You would have forgotten it within minutes, or you would have found it human, even endearing.

Third, move your attention outward. Self-consciousness grows when all our attention points inward. Curiosity about the other person, about the task, about the moment, is one of the gentlest ways to turn the spotlight off.

sections.heading: A Smaller Stage
sections.text:
It can feel a little humbling to realise that we are not at the center of everyone's attention. But it is also a relief.

The stage you feel you are standing on is much smaller, and much kinder, than it seems. The audience is mostly busy with its own lines. And the people who do notice you are often more forgiving than the critic inside your head.

So the next time you trip on a step, or say the wrong word, let the moment pass. Almost everyone else already has.

short.title: Why you feel watched – and almost nobody is
short.text:
In a famous experiment at Cornell University, students had to walk into a room wearing an embarrassing T-shirt. They guessed that about half the people noticed it. In reality, only around a quarter did.

Psychologists call this the spotlight effect. We feel watched because we are the center of our own experience. But everyone else is busy being the center of theirs.

And there is more. After a first conversation, people consistently underestimate how much the other person liked them.

So the next time you say something awkward, let it go. Almost everyone else already has.
